beats.say: Here's a strange thing.
You ask a chatbot about your company's refund policy. It answers instantly. Clear. Confident. Polite.
And the rule it just gave you... does not exist.
How can a machine make something up, with a straight face? By the end of this video, you'll know exactly why. And you'll know the one thing you control to keep it in line.
Chapter one. How a large language model actually works.
Let's start with something you use every day.
Type: see you, on your phone. The keyboard suggests: tomorrow.
It doesn't understand you. It has just seen, see you tomorrow, so many times that tomorrow is the most likely next word.
Now imagine that keyboard has read... almost the entire internet.
That's it. That's a large language model. A machine that predicts the next piece of text.
So how does it get so good at guessing? Practice. Trillions of tiny quizzes.
Hide the next word. Let the model guess. Wrong? Nudge its internal dials, just a little.
Those dials are called parameters. Big models have billions of them.

Repeat that trillions of times, and something surprising happens. To guess Paris, it had to learn a fact. To guess the next line of a maths problem, it had to learn something that looks like reasoning.
Nobody taught it facts. Facts were just useful for guessing the next word.
But here's the catch. Remember this one sentence, because it explains almost every failure you'll ever see.
It writes what is likely. Not what is checked.
Usually, likely and true are the same thing. When they're not, you get that confident, made-up refund rule.
One more detail. The model doesn't actually read words. It reads chunks, a bit like Lego bricks.
Refund might be two bricks: ref, and und. Milk is just one.
These bricks are called tokens. And each one is really just a number.
Handy rule: a hundred tokens is about seventy-five English words.
This solves a puzzle from finance: why does the same question cost more in Marathi?
The box of bricks was built mostly from English. English words fit in a few big bricks. Marathi needs lots of small ones.
And you pay per brick. Same question. Bigger bill.
Now, a mystery.
Meera runs support. She asked the chatbot the same question twice, and got two different answers.
Here's why. When the model picks the next word, it doesn't have one answer. It has a list of options, each with a chance.
Within: sixty-two percent. Only: twenty-one percent. And a long tail of others.
And then... it spins the wheel.
That spin is called sampling. One spin, for every single word.
So if an early spin lands on only, instead of within, the whole answer heads somewhere else.
Same question. Different spin. Different answer. Mystery solved.
And you control the wheel, with a dial called temperature.
Turn it down, and the favourite slice grows. Answers become predictable.
Turn it up, and the slices even out. Answers get creative. Sometimes, a little weird.
At zero, there's no spin at all. It always takes the favourite.
There's also a pair of scissors called top p. It cuts away the tiny, absurd slices before the spin.
So: refund rules? Low temperature. Ten catchy email subject lines? Turn it up.

One thing interviewers love: even at zero, a hosted model isn't perfectly repeatable. Tiny rounding differences on shared chips can flip a near tie. So pin the model version, and expect small variations.
Back to that invented refund rule.
The model learned from the public internet. FreshCart's refund policy? Private. It was never in there.
So when you ask about it, the model does what it always does: it writes the most likely-sounding answer.
A generic, believable refund rule. Fluent. Confident. Wrong. This is called a hallucination.
Can't we just train it on our policies? Usually, no. Training teaches habits and style well, but facts learned that way are fuzzy, and you'd retrain every time a policy changes.

Quick detour. How does a next-word predictor become a helpful chatbot? First, pretraining: read the internet, predict next words. Ask that raw model a question, and it might just continue with more questions.
Then instruction tuning: thousands of examples of good answers.
Then preference training: people pick the better of two answers. That's where the polite, helpful tone comes from.
And newer reasoning models get rewarded for getting maths and code right, so they learn to think step by step before answering.
Quick question for you. Why would a longer prompt cost more, even when the answer is short? Think about it for a second.
To answer that, let's peek inside.
First, every token becomes a list of numbers: its spot on a giant map of meaning. Words used in similar ways land close together.
Now the clever part. Take this sentence: The milk was spoiled, so the customer returned it.
What does it mean? You know instantly: the milk. The model works it out by letting it look back at every earlier word, and shine a light on the ones that matter.
That's called attention.
Stack dozens of these layers, each one refining the meaning, and out the other end comes... the spinning wheel for the next word.
Now the cost question answers itself. Before writing a single word, every token of your prompt goes through every layer. And attention compares each token with all the ones before it.
Double the prompt, and the work more than doubles.
It's also why you can't paste in all twelve thousand company documents. They won't fit in the model's context window: the most text it can handle at once.
And even when it fits, things buried in the middle of a huge prompt get overlooked.
So what can you actually control?
You can't retrain it. You can't paste in everything. What's left is the prompt: the instructions you send with every request.
First real task: three thousand support tickets a day, sorted by hand into refund, late delivery, missing item, and other.
Attempt one: a single line of instructions. Eighty-one percent correct. Not bad.
Then people start adding patches. IMPORTANT! Refunds are not complaints! And every patch breaks something else.
Here's what works. Brief it like a smart new colleague on day one.
Who it is, and what the goal is.
Clear definitions, especially for the confusing cases.
A few examples, picked from the hard ones. That's called few-shot prompting.
And exactly what shape the answer should take.
Same model. Ninety-three percent.
No magic words. Clear instructions, good examples, and testing every change against those labelled tickets. Prompting, done well, is engineering.
Let's lock it in.
An LLM predicts the next token.
It picks by spinning a weighted wheel, and temperature shapes that wheel.
It writes what's likely, not what's checked, so it hallucinates about things it never saw.
Attention lets each word look back at the words that matter.
And the prompt is your steering wheel.
But Meera wants the real thing now: answers from FreshCart's actual policies.
Only two or three pages, out of twelve thousand documents, matter for each question. If you could find those pages first, in a split second... what would you do with them?
That's chapter two. See you there.
